130. ◑ DESIGN DONE 2026-09-01 (docs/design/130-stream-reactive-types.md; v1 per the spec below). Hard-parts decided: single-consumer v1 (multicast refused, bridge is the escape); cancellation owned by the subscription owner (its LIFO stack); provider death delivers a terminal event Closed/Faulted never silent Pending; bounded-buffer backpressure with an explicit policy (default error, no silent loss); replay only if the provider declares replay(n)/replay(from durable); six-tier protocol subscribe/next/close with py/ts async, go/java/rust blocking cancel-select, and wasm REFUSING (same honest EmitError as awaited steps); effectful callbacks allowed in the every body (G1/G8 checked, A8 on failure); cross-realm only via an explicit bridge; crash recovery non-reconstructible by default (reported as teardown-contract unreconstructible residue) unless a durable replay cursor is declared. Typed events are a Stream[T] SPECIALIZATION not a distinct surface (event schema=G1, on..as desugars to every..in subscribe), deferred to slice 5. Slice split: S1 [landable, no dep] Stream[T]+Stream[T,State]+subscribe/next/close+bracket lifecycle+core-guarantee tests, parser+typecheck+lower, py full / wasm refuses / ts if free; S2 map/filter/take+backpressure+test-clock; S3 merge+go/java/rust blocking lowerings; S4 every..in async iteration (needs item 131); S5 typed events. Adversarial review CRITICAL: a consumer parked in next on a silently-dead provider makes the bracket inverse close unreachable (deadlock on blocking tiers, fiber leak on event-loop tiers), violating the core guarantee; fixed by cancellation-first next (next awaits a race of item-vs-cancel-token, close trips the token synchronously on every tier) + admission rule 3.6 refusing any provider that can vanish without delivering a terminal. **`Stream[T]` reactive types.** A verified reactive sequence: a stream provider emits values over time, a consumer processes them as they arrive; provider teardown closes the stream, consumer teardown releases the subscription (LIFO). The language-level form of reactive coeffects for event-driven sagas (Kafka/webhooks/real-time). Needs its own lifecycle story on six tiers. Builds on the reactive coeffect model + provide/inject graph. ~3-4 wk. High novelty. 

    **v1 design spec (from an external proposal, verified: no Stream type exists yet).** Do NOT start with a general reactive calculus. v1 = `Stream[T]` + a small API (`subscribe`/`next`/`close`/`map`/`filter`/`take`/`merge`) and an `every x in subscription { ... }` async-iteration form. Support ONLY: one consumer, explicit `close`, bounded buffering, a deterministic test-time clock, documented refusals for unsupported tiers/shapes; NO implicit multicast, NO automatic retry. Model the subscription as an `acquire`/`undo` resource with an optional state type `Stream[T, State]` (Created->Active->Paused->Closed). CORE GUARANTEE: every admitted stream subscription has an explicit cancellation path, and unloading its owner closes the stream before the owner disappears (a natural extension of acquire/undo + G5/G7/A8 LIFO teardown). Hard-parts to DECIDE before implementing: single-consumer vs multicast (start single), cancellation ownership (the subscription owner), provider-death behavior (consumer becomes Pending or gets a terminal event), backpressure (bounded buffer + explicit policy), replay (only if the provider declares it), the common minimal six-tier protocol (wasm has no async, so it REFUSES streams like it refuses timers), effectful callbacks (allowed but capability+lifecycle checked), cross-realm (only via an explicit bridge), crash recovery (recreate the subscription or mark it non-reconstructible). Blast radius: parser + typecheck + lower + all six backends + async-coloring (A1/106). Design-first, ~3-4 wk. 

    **+ typed external EVENTS (external proposal #10, folded here).** A first-class event contract (`event OrderCreated { order_id: Str, timestamp: Int }`, `on OrderCreated as event { ... }`) with the checker verifying schema compatibility, consumer lifecycle, duplicate handling, event ownership, replay behavior, handler idempotency, and that a failed handler does not leave a subscription active. Related to this Stream[T] item (an event is a stream item with a contract); decide whether events are a distinct surface or a Stream specialization. Useful for queues, MCP notifications, WebSockets, IoT.

138. ✅ **`revl import cordis` refuses/mis-parses DSH's LEADING-PIPE & multiline union style (re-filed from agent/harness-m3 finding #37; follow-on to 137).** Item 137's `Branded`->`Str` and literal-union->variant both work, but the real DSH `PluginFiberPhase` is formatted leading-pipe-per-member across lines and still fails, two ways: (a) a LEADING-PIPE union (`type X =` newline `| 'a'` newline `| 'b'`) refuses — the union parser doesn't strip the empty/leading fragment when splitting on `|` ("no revl spelling for the TypeScript type '| 'pending''"); fix: drop empty/leading fragments on the `|` split. 161. ✅ (py-tier reference; per-tier emitter routing → 167) **stdlib `Router`/`RoundRobin` load-balancer component — load balancing as spawn+realms+router, verified.** The G2 resolution for load balancing: N workers each `spawn`ed into their OWN local realm (G2 holds per-(key,realm), one `db` per realm), and a single `Router` component that `requires db in realm("w1")…realm("wN")` and `provides db` in the parent realm — so consumers see ONE provider (G2 holds) and the router distributes. Deliver a stdlib component `RoundRobin[T](n: Int, factory: T)` (and/or `LoadBalancer`) that spawns a pool (`spawn_pool(n, factory)` with `undo dispose_pool`), provides `T` by routing (round-robin / least-loaded) to the workers, and gets reactive failover FOR FREE: a dead worker's coeffect suspends its route (R2/R3, peer-death monitor), survivors continue; a replacement re-activates. Usage: `requires db via RoundRobin[Database](3, PgDatabase)`. Written IN revl, verified by the gate (its own acquire/route/dispose lifecycle is checked by G7/A8 — a load balancer that provably can't orphan workers). Builds on: spawn (all 6 tiers ✅), local realms per-spawn ✅, reactive coeffects ✅, peer-death monitor ✅, TCP+mTLS ✅ (workers can be cross-machine, cross-tier). `stdlib/` new component. Effort ~3-5 days (primitives exist; this packages them). **NON-GOAL (do NOT do): a language-level `provide db with multiplicity(3)`** — two providers of one key in one realm breaks G2 and destroys verification; the router pattern is the required shape.

162. ✅ (frontend slice — runtime routing deferred to 161) **Multi-realm `require` syntax — `requires db in realms("w1","w2","w3") strategy(round_robin)`.** Additive extension of the existing `requires <key> in realm(<name>)` binding to a realm LIST + an optional routing strategy, so a consumer (the Router of item 161, or any consumer) binds all N realms at once and routes across them. The compiler verifies EACH named realm has a provider of the key (G2 per-realm still holds — one provider per realm). Parser change (the realm-list is an extension of the single-realm concept), plus lexer/typecheck/lower for the N-way bind and the strategy annotation. Complements item 161 (the Router consumes this). Effort ~1 week, additive. `src/revl/parser.py` (+lexer/typecheck/lower). Depends on nothing new; the runtime multi-bind is the reactive coeffect model already in place.

163. ✅ **Doc/framing: the revl distribution model — load balancing = spawn+realms+router, the constraint IS the feature.** Document the design decision (so no future contributor naively breaks it): G2 (one key, one provider, one realm) and load balancing are in DIRECT tension, and the resolution is spawn+realms+router (items 161/162), NOT multiple providers. Record the two NON-GOALS explicitly: (a) NO language-level multiplicity construct (`provide … with multiplicity(N)`) — it breaks G2 and turns a verified composition language into an unverified distributed system; (b) revl ships NO built-in LB infrastructure (no Envoy/Nginx/HAProxy) — the router is a revl component you compose, the algorithm is its implementation detail, the transport is TCP+mTLS, placement decides the host. Include the distribution-model table (spawn=instances, named realms=sharding, router+pool=LB, reactive coeffects=failover, TCP+mTLS=remote, quarantine=circuit-breaking, revl_resolve=registry multi-resolution). The payoff line: a load balancer whose OWN lifecycle is compile-time verified — something no service mesh offers. `docs/` (a distribution-model design doc). Effort ~0.5-1 day.

168. ✅ **Self-host gate's statement reader is LINE-BASED — single-line bodies diverge from the reference + fuzzers only emit multi-line (oracle-coverage gap; from item 166).** `selfhost/lower.rvl` reads statements line-by-line (mirroring `checker.rvl`), so a component body whose statements share ONE source line diverges from py `lower.py`: e.g. `{ let store = effect Map.new() undo store.drop() isolate d in realm("r1") provide s {…} }` → reference refuses `PRELUDE`, the gate ADMITS (the `let` line swallows the trailing `isolate`/`provide`). Slice D derived sinks + B3/B4 [state-threading, fn-value signatures] remain) (Slice B propagation fixpoint landed — the relay-laundering injection exploit now refused at G9; Slice C endorsement + Slice D sinks remain) (docs/design/249-taint-provenance.md: Slice B propagation fixed-point, Slice C endorse[origin] granted declassification, Slice D granting-side sinks; proves the relay-laundering exploit compiles today) **Taint and provenance — prompt-injection defense derived from the
    effect system.** The agent-security failure of the era (the "lethal
    trifecta": untrusted input + private data + an outbound channel) is
    an *information-flow* problem, and revl already draws every boundary
    it needs: emissions and externs are exactly where values enter and
    leave the composition. Extend classification from *crossings* to
    *values*: what returns across a boundary is **tainted with its
    origin** (`web:example.com`, `model`, `fs:workspace`), taint
    propagates through pure computation (a fixed point over the same
    call graph the capability analysis walks), and the dangerous edge —
    a tainted value flowing into the *arguments of another emission* —
    becomes a checked event: allowed, policy-gated (33: "web-tainted
    values may not reach `send.*` without ack"), or refused. Two
    payoffs land immediately in the lighthouse workload: (a) tool results
    carry their taint into the model context, so a harness can render
    untrusted spans as untrusted to the model and the operator; (b) the
    exfiltration pattern — web content steering a send — is a *gate
    event with a why-trace*, not a hope about prompt wording. Honest
    scope from day one: taint is tracked in the runtime value
    representation on hosted tiers (dynamic, like the Int bound), the
    static half is an over-approximation (the audit already is), and
    the G8 caveat applies — a lying extern classification lies about
    taint too. Nobody has typed information flow in an agent harness;
    revl is one fixed point away from it.
 

    **+ input trust labels (external proposal #10, folded here).** Explicit `Untrusted[Str]` / `Trusted[Policy]` types; the checker REFUSES `Untrusted[Str] -> shell command`, `-> capability name`, `-> policy update` unless an explicit sanitizer or approval step intervenes. The principled prompt-injection answer: untrusted input cannot DIRECTLY create authority (stronger than an LLM 'ignore malicious text' instruction).
 

    **+ Fable: design/reconciliation FIRST - the item folds TWO mechanisms (dynamic runtime taint + static Untrusted[Str]/Trusted[Policy] labels) with no decision on which is v1, what a sanitizer/declassification step is, or how they compose. The RUNTIME taint half edits the same six-tier value-representation seam as 243 Slice 2, so it queues behind Slice 2. Static half + design-doc runnable now.**

    prompt-count collapses with it. `stdlib/shell.rvl` + the

253. ◑ SLICE 1 LANDED 2026-09-01 (Temporal emission target, merged 232a494 + golden typecheck shim f6155fd: an emit(ir, target="temporal") seam emitting the workflow/activity split, the derived write-ahead saga, and the two-phase LIFO drain with a workflow-side compensation budget, faithful at-most-once [maximumAttempts:1] matching the revl runtime, plus a residue-query envelope. Slice 2 evidence-derived retries + real SDK/cluster integration deferred). DESIGN DONE (docs/design/253-temporal-target.md). **A Temporal emission target — the saga framework arrives with an
    installed base.** (Suggested by a worker agent; accepted with an
    alignment that makes it stronger than it first looks.) Temporal's
    two cardinal rules — workflow code must be deterministic, IO
    belongs only in activities — are *exactly* revl's stratum
    discipline: pure/effect code is the workflow, emissions are the
    activities, and revl checks at compile time the rule Temporal can
    only document and hope. So `revl emit --target temporal` (a target
    *variant* over the existing py/ts emitters — not an eighth
    runtime): a component's activation becomes a workflow, each
    `effect … undo …` registers its inverse in a compensation chain
    whose LIFO order is G7-derived (the code Temporal users write by
    hand and get wrong), `compensate` (247) maps onto Temporal's own
    best-effort idiom, and item 44's idempotency evidence configures
    activity retry policies *safely* — retries only where the type
    system says retry is sound. What the target buys free: durable
    execution (Temporal's history is item 47's WAL, operated by
    someone else), timers (57), signals (48), production retries — and
    a distribution channel: "keep your Temporal cluster; write the
    workflow in revl; the compensation chain is derived and the
    determinism rule is a compile error." Honest scope, stated first:
    this is *the durable-workflow subset* — realms, hot-swap and
    reactive withdrawal do not map in v1 (workflow versioning may
    carry drift-checked upgrades later, its own design note); a
    composition using them is refused for this target with a
    why-trace, never silently narrowed. Spec-first: the mapping table
    (component/effect/emission/fault ↔ workflow/compensation/activity/
    failure) is the design doc, and the exit test is one saga demo
    running on a real Temporal dev server with an injected mid-saga
    fault compensating in derived order.

DESIGN DONE (docs/design/254-witnessed-network.md). **Witnessed network effects — the reversible boundary pushed into
    the wire, endpoint by endpoint, with evidence.** Item 243 moved
    the reversible/irreversible boundary for the filesystem by
    engineering witnesses; the same move works on APIs whose semantics
    permit it: a PUT with a GET-preimage is a witnessed write (undo =
    PUT the preimage back), a DELETE against a recreate-capable
    endpoint is a witnessed remove, a POST to a resource with a
    documented delete is `compensate`-grade, and everything else stays
    an honest emission. The evidence rule is the import family's,
    unchanged: witnessed status is *declared per endpoint* and flows
    from documented semantics (RFC 9110 idempotency via item 44,
    `x-revl-*` annotations in `import openapi`), never inferred from
    optimism — and the generated header states claim vs proof exactly
    as OpenAPI import already does. The §4.1 caveat is *stronger*
    over a network and the module must say so: reversal does not undo
    observation, and remote observers are the common case, not the
    edge. Payoff where it lands: the workload's outbound HTTP tooling
    stops being all-emission the same way its fs tooling did
    (243/244), and item 248's measurement extends to the network
    boundary — the
    fraction of an agent's API traffic that became witnessed or
    compensable, per session, with proof.

    The model call is the one emission whose response the whole system
    then *executes*, and today it returns `Str` — every tool-call
    parse is stringly, every malformed response is a bespoke bug.
    Declare the response type instead: `emission fn complete(prompt:
    Ctx) -> AgentTurn` where `AgentTurn` is an ADT (`Final(text) |
    ToolCalls(List[Call])`), the JSON schema is **derived from the
    type** (the MCP schema machinery already maps revl types to JSON
    Schema — run it at this boundary too), the provider extern passes
    the schema to constrained decoding where the API supports it and
    validates the response against it regardless, and a malformed
    response is a *typed fault* — retryable, because a completion is
    classified safe-to-retry (a read with a cost, item 44's evidence
    vocabulary), with the retry budget declared, not hoped. Downstream
    the agent loop stops parsing: it matches. The general principle is
    bigger than the model: any emission may declare a structured
    response type and get boundary validation derived from it — the
    model is just the emission where it pays most.

Spec only, implementation follows) **Witness retention — the undo horizon, stated.** The witnessed
    world (243/244) accumulates preimages: every write keeps a
    snapshot, every rm keeps the file, and nothing yet says when a
    witness may be dropped. Unbounded, that is a storage bill; bounded
    naively, it is a silent lie — dropping a witness retroactively
    downgrades an effect from witnessed to irreversible, which is a
    *class change* and must never happen quietly. Make retention a
    declared policy with an honest surface: witnesses live to the
    commit horizon by default (commit garbage-collects the witnesses
    of committed effects — the deferral queue (245) already knows
    which those are), generation retention (65) and session branching
    (250) extend the horizon explicitly, a size budget may force early
    drops **only through the same class-change accounting**, and the
    audit answers "how far back can this composition actually revert,
    right now?" with a horizon marker ("undo horizon: commit N−3;
    witnesses dropped beyond: 2, listed"). The rule in one line: a
    witness may be dropped, but the *proof surface must say so before
    anyone relies on it* — same honesty contract as replay §4.

Mechanism, now exact: `selfhost/lexer.rvl` threads `source` as a PARAMETER through ~12 per-token helpers, so a per-function shadow is a per-CALL `chars().collect()` — O(calls·n) of ALLOCATION traded for O(calls·i) of iteration. A `pub` callee demands nothing of its callers (it collects its own view). The retraction is what makes it non-regressing: a viewed slot whose argument at some in-module call site is not an already-viewed parameter is BANNED and the fixpoint recomputed, so NO in-module call site gains a collect — the emitted lexer holds exactly one `chars().collect()`, in `lex_src` (`count_nl`/`radix_value` retract and keep the walk over their short slices). ## The embeddable compiler: revl as a safety kernel (post-v3.0 arc)

These build on two settled results. First, the self-hosted compiler is a
PURE-FUNCTION pipeline (`selfhost/compile.rvl`: `admit(source) -> verdict`,
`compile_to(source, tier) -> output`, no cordis dependency), already compiled
and run natively on py + rust (items 283/284 profiled its rust runtime). Second,
per-tool-call witnessed effects + session commit + six-tier crash recovery
shipped (243/244/245/322). Together they turn revl from "a language with a CLI"
into an admission gate you EMBED in any host runtime. The remaining lever the arc
depends on is the self-host coverage frontier: the function/type surface is
byte-exact today, the component/method-body surface is the `revl`-column `lim`
frontier in docs/conformance.md.

The design's go/no-go spike RESOLVED YES: cordis-rs 0.3 and the whole generated `revl-gate` crate cross-compile clean to wasm32, so the rust lane carries the gate to the edge with no vendoring and no upstream fork. Shipped: a `revl:gate@1.0.0` WASI-P2 component exporting Cut A as `admit` / `admit-json` / `gate-version`, plus `admit-artifact` present and failing closed. MEASURED: 317,203 bytes, an EMPTY import section, 1,525,847 wasmtime fuel for one `admit` over a one-line program, ~85s cold build - against the playground's 1.4 MB wheel plus a Pyodide runtime, which is the cost baseline this item exists to beat. TWO CORRECTIONS TO THE DESIGN, both measured, neither a scope change: (a) the target is wasm32-unknown-unknown and NOT wasm32-wasip2, because on wasip2 rust's std links the WASI world into every artifact and the import section is then not empty, and the empty-import property is the load-bearing one (it is what makes a verdict provably a function of its arguments); (b) the .wasm is NOT committed under a byte-difference drift gate, because a rust binary is byte-reproducible only against one exact toolchain - what is committed and drift-gated is the crate SOURCE plus an exactly-pinned wit-bindgen, and the conformance vector is computed live from the reference in-process, which is 'at the build sha' by construction and cannot go stale. Also measured: on every wasm target rust's panic strategy is `abort`, so the crate's catch_unwind fail-closed path does not catch and a native gate panic TRAPS instead of returning outside-frontier; a trap is neither a verdict nor an admission, and the vector requires zero of them. REMAINING: slice 3 (`admit-artifact`, the 289 chain) is blocked on the chain's MIDDLE set - the declared caps are the G8 boundary projection, which the reference derives with a whole-IR reachability walk (`revl.__main__._boundary`) that has no native port, and a guessed declared set would be exactly the wave-through this arc exists to prevent; slice 4 (jco transpile + a browser/serverless harness showing the double enforcement). 342. ✅ **A single repair/agent loop cannot serve both a sync and an async caller — no sync/async arrow polymorphism (lighthouse-workload finding; the dual of item 92).** Item 92 resolved the async-callback-value problem by having the loop declare its callback async-typed (`complete: (List[Msg]) -> Async[Str]`, resolution (c)), so `author_repair(goal, budget, complete, compile)` in the lighthouse workload's self-evolver is async-parameterized and drives the async `SelfEvolver.author` (where `model.complete` is an `emission async fn`). H19 then needed the SAME repair loop from the agent's tool surface — `ToolRegistry.call`, a NON-async `emission fn` — where the model crossing is genuinely SYNCHRONOUS (a blocking HTTP POST / a scripted read). Two walls: (a) A1 refuses reaching an async op from the sync method, and (b) a sync arrow `(List[Msg]) -> Str` is refused where `(List[Msg]) -> Async[Str]` is expected ("only an arrow may be passed into an async parameter"). So the async-typed loop is UNREACHABLE from the sync caller, and the workload had to duplicate it as `author_repair_sync` (identical control flow, sharing `repair_prompt`/`model_reply_text`; only the arrow color differs). The `Async[Str]` return the design chose for item 92 is now the thing that prevents reuse across the two call sites the same harness naturally has (an async evolve path AND a sync tool-call path over ONE loop). Fix directions: (a) sync/async POLYMORPHISM over a callback parameter — a loop generic in whether `complete` suspends, monomorphized per call site (the caller's color decides), so `author_repair` serves both; or (b) allow a sync `(…) -> T` arrow to satisfy a `(…) -> Async[T]` parameter (a sync value trivially lifts into a completed async), colored at the call site; either removes the duplicate. Repro: one `fn loop(c: (X) -> Async[Y], …)` called once with `x => emit async_op(x)` from an `async fn` and once with `x => emit sync_op(x)` from a sync `emission fn` — the second is refused, forcing a sync twin. `src/revl/lower.py`/`typecheck.py`/`emission_analysis.py` (arrow-color polymorphism / sync-lifts-to-async coercion). LOW-MED (one duplicated loop per shared sync+async workload; the workaround is mechanical).

Either land the capability-scope slot on emission externs (so realm-style tokens like `gateway.send` work uniformly with `witnessed[caps]` and the 33 policy grammar) or correct `docs/design/245-session-commit.md` Decision 2's examples and state the name-is-the-capability rule in a consumer-facing place. COMPLETED ON THE POLICY-REACH AXIS 2026-09-03 (PR #257, closes #247): 343 landed the `emission[caps]` slot and made the approval `ClassMap` key a scoped crossing by its DECLARED TOKEN, but `__main__._boundary` was never given the same treatment and kept a directly-emitted extern's own NAME as host reach. `policy.component_reach` reads that surface, so the two halves of one rule sat in different namespaces — `audit_diff._capability_registers` keys the floor input `db` while the selector saw `pg_write` — and `capability db requires register keyed` selected nothing on a composition whose only `db` crossing was a direct emission. Found while landing #245, where the design note's two-extern reproducer never reached the refusal and the end-to-end test had to add a service method to make the rule fire. The decision recorded: reach carries the declared token (`capabilities or (name,)`, the rule `lower._extern_emission_caps`, the witnessed seed, `_capability_registers` and the approval fold all already used), and a scoped extern's NAME is NOT a policy token — one spelling per crossing, not two. `_boundary`'s per-component `externs` entries carry the declared scope (absent when unscoped, so every pre-247 audit document is byte-identical) and the `host code:` line renders it as `pg_write [db] (emission, py)`. Blast radius measured over the whole corpus: 7 components in 6 files of the 604 compilable `.rvl` documents change reach, no composition changed admission verdict, and the only red was the 414 harness asserting the old namespace — its `component_reach` and approval cells now agree on the token. `tests/test_247_capability_reach_spellings.py` pins the whole spelling table so which spelling puts a token under policy is read, not discovered by experiment; docs/boundary-policy.md gained "Which spelling a rule selects" and docs/capabilities.md §2/§5 the scoped-extern rows. NOT changed and recorded here rather than silently: `audit_diff.crossings`' `host:<component>:<name>` drift token and `cardinality`'s per-capability ceilings stay keyed by extern name (they enumerate host code, not authority), and the approval fold reads a BARE emission's required KEY where `_boundary` records `*` — a separate question about bare emissions, not decided here.

344. ✅ LANDED (was 🚧; standing grants + revl_approve on main, revocable via 379) [agent/344-standing-approval: TTL/uses-scoped standing grant via revl_approve against a capability (fork b) - 3 per-call prompts -> 1] ✅ (session-scoped standing approval fork b: revl_approve mints a TTL/uses grant per capability; per-call class-(c) crossings consume it instead of prompting - H4 shell-escape 3->1; policy-off byte-identical) **GAP (found by the 248 harness measurement): `await approval` is activation-body-only, so a per-TOOL-CALL typed approval cannot exist — the `requires approval [ttl]` surface is unreachable for exactly the calls an agent harness wants it for.** An agent tool's class-(c) crossing happens per call, mid-session, in provide-method position; `await approval[C] { fields }` is refused there ("only allowed in a component activation body … a provide method runs while the component is ACTIVE (item 246)"). Consequence, verified end to end: declaring `requires approval` on a per-call extern makes the consuming component UNADMITTABLE (no approval edge can be written in a method; fail-closed exactly as 246 open question 3 predicts), so the typed invariants — the TTL above all — cannot govern tool crossings. The operator-layer ticket two-step covers the per-call need minus the standing-grant half (every (c) call prompts, single-use, exact-hash; that is what the 248 measurement used, `perCall` = 1 per unique (c) call). The missing shape is a SESSION-scoped standing approval an operator mints once and tool calls consume against ("approve `term.shell` for 10m / for n uses"), hash-bound and expiring like the typed token but not threaded through `with` in source — i.e. the 251 distillation target, needed one item early. Design fork: (a) allow `await approval` in method position (suspend the call fiber on the 246 MCP seam — the seam already parks call futures), or (b) TTL/uses-scoped ledger entries mintable via `revl_approve` against a capability rather than one ticket hash. 350. ◑ REVL SIDE LANDED (`feat/350-environment-binding`): the exit surface exists — `boot component X { config { … } }` IS the environment contract (one per composition, refused at link if two; not spawnable), `revl run --env FILE` is its ONE door (a `--config` table naming the boot component is refused, an undeclared `--env` key is refused rather than dropped, a missing required field refuses the boot before any runtime is imported), the MCP `revl_load` seam enforces the same value-level rules (it has one config channel, so a boot entry there IS the env injection: undeclared key / wrong type / out-of-bound all refused before the runtime is touched, closing what would otherwise be an inject-past-the-bounds door), and the contract is published by `revl audit` (a valueless name/type/required/secret/bound table) with an `env:<name>:<bound>` drift crossing so a NEW field or a DROPPED bound reads as a widening. The authority half beyond the item's own exit: a contract field may declare an admission bound (`under "<prefix>"` for a path, `in [...]` for an enumerated choice), checked against the injected value, because an environment value adds no capability but DOES spell a resource scope (a data dir is the path reached, a provider identity is the destination posted to) — so an unbounded one widens the real reach while the declared capability set and the audit stay unchanged. A bound outside a boot component is refused: unenforced grammar would be the same fail-open. Additive and conditional throughout (a composition with no boot component is byte-identical through parse, IR, manifest, audit and every tier); the self-host gate is ported (`at_boot`/`boot_names` in `selfhost/lower.rvl`, the new BOOT tag in the differential oracle) so the native rust gate does not admit what the reference refuses. TWO EDGES STATED, NOT CLOSED, both in docs/environment-binding.md: (a) a host can still route an environment-read value through a NON-boot component's `--config` — the composition-bootstrap floor, since the host compiles and plugs; the contract removes the silence, not the trust; (b) `under` is LEXICAL (the preflight must not touch the filesystem), so a symlink inside the prefix still points wherever it points — that needs a runtime enforcer, item 411's lane. REMAINING: harness-side adoption (revl-harness's own roadmap) — `_config()`'s data-dir/model/secret-dir derivation moving behind a `boot` component. docs/environment-binding.md + syntax-2.0 §6.2 + examples/environment_contract.rvl; tests/test_environment_binding_350.py. **GAP (harness-in-revl, found by the revl-harness dogfood goal): environment binding — tokens, data-dir paths, and model choice are read before the composition exists.** The host must know the port, the auth token, the data dir, and which model provider to boot before it can compile the composition; these flow in through component `config {}` blocks and env injection at plug time (the sanctioned seam). The composition itself now lives in revl (manifest.rvl + composition.rvl ship/revert), but "the thing that decides the port" is host. Exit: a revl `boot` component that declares the environment contract (what the host must inject), so the boundary is explicit and audited instead of implicit py. LOW effort, MED harness benefit. <!-- auto-revl-harness:environment-binding-is-host -->

361. ✅ **An ASYNC provide method cannot use a match BLOCK arm (only expression arms), and module fns cannot carry the async color — so multi-step conditional async logic is forced into one nested expression-if pipeline (revl-harness CLI-engine provider dogfood).** Writing the harness's `EngineModel.complete` (an `async` provide method that must refuse a non-engine provider, check binary availability, spawn, and branch on the raw reply) hit two interacting limits: (a) a match BLOCK arm (`=> { let …; expr }`) refuses in a provide-method body — "a block-bodied match arm is not lowerable here; block arms lower inside a module `fn` body" (parser.py `_match_block_arm` + the G6 rule that provide bodies are pure expressions: statement `if`/`return` are equally refused) — and (b) a module `fn` reaching an async extern is refused (item 90's phase-2 rule, still open: "a module fn body reaching an async extern is refused"), so the block CANNOT be lifted into a helper `fn` that calls `engine_run`. Net effect: the whole multi-step conditional body became one nested `if (…) { … } else { … }` expression pipeline (workable, tests green on py+ts, but hard to read and it recurs in every async provider that needs conditionals). Fix options, in preference order: (1) let module `fn` bodies carry the async color (item 90 phase 2) so a match block arm can be lifted into an async helper — the expression arm + binding ALREADY works today (verified: `Some(e) => ping("…"+e)` calls the async extern in a provide method), the gap is only the BLOCK form; (2) lower match block arms inside provide-method bodies directly (lift into an inline async lambda rather than refusing). Repro lives in revl-harness `src/components/engine_model.rvl` (`complete`). `src/revl/parser.py` + `lower.py` + `emission_analysis.py`.

362. ✅ **A total (never-raising) JSON parse — `json_parse` today raises on non-JSON input, and revl has no try/catch, so every *tolerant* JSON walk (skip bad lines, continue on malformed) must be a classified extern (revl-harness CLI-engine provider dogfood; the design doc already names the replacement).** `stdlib/json.rvl`'s `json_parse(s) -> Any` is `@py { json.loads(s) }` — it RAISES on invalid input, and revl's design excludes `try/catch` (docs/syntax-2.0.md §3.2: "failure is `Result` in pure code"), so a component cannot walk a JSONL stream and skip non-JSON lines in-language. The harness's `parse_engine_output` (engine_run.rvl) is therefore a classified extern whose per-engine extraction (which field = the final answer for claude/codex/opencode/droid/copilot) is FORCED into host code purely by the raising parse — the shape knowledge is policy that belongs in revl. **The designed spelling already exists as the answer:** change `json_parse` (or add `json_try_parse`) to return `Result[Any, Str]` (or `Opt[Any]`) instead of raising — `Ok(v)` on valid JSON, `Err(reason)` on invalid — so `match json_parse(line) { Ok(v) => …, Err(_) => skip }` walks a stream tolerantly IN REVL, with the classify-extern rule unchanged for genuine host power (subprocess stays an extern by design; this item is only about the parse). Then the harness's `parse_engine_output` can be rewritten as a pure revl fn (`raw.split(NL)` — `Str.split` already exists — then per-line `match`, then per-engine field reads off the parsed record, which typed access already supports), deleting the duplicated @py/@ts parser bodies and their tier-divergence surface (a py/ts divergence in the plain branch was caught this session). Byte-compat: the `Ok`-carrying path is byte-identical to today's successful parse; only the error channel changes. `stdlib/json.rvl` + `src/revl/typecheck.py` (the `Any` extern return and its matchability) + backends as needed for the Result/Any plumbing. ~small; the design doc has already reserved this exact shape.

363. ✅ LANDED (per-component `[tiers]`/`[processes]` placement is implemented and the six F1-F6 tier-placement holes found by the 2026-08-31 review are closed, merged a85e431; test_tier_placement 17 + test_tier_placement_hardening 13 green). Design: docs/design/363-per-component-tier-placement.md: [tiers] manifest table, existing cross-process seam, per-process emission slice + tier-capability gate, cross-tier witnessed rollback scoped out; headline rust/go) **Per-component TIER placement — declare which backend a component emits to, so a hot worker compiles to rust/go/wasm while the rest of the composition stays on py/ts (revl-harness CLI-engine provider request; complements 173, NOT auto-optimization).** revl's distribution model (`docs/distribution-model.md`) places components across PROCESSES by realm/host (spawn + realms + router + TCP+mTLS), and the whole composition emits to ONE tier per run (`revl run --backend py|ts|rust|go|java|wasm`). There is no way to say "this component is CPU-bound, emit IT to rust, keep everything else on py/ts" — per-component tier choice is neither syntax nor a placement mode. This item adds an EXPLICIT, declared placement hint, not automatic per-component optimization (the docs deliberately decline auto-tier selection: the distribution model warns the naive "compile each piece to its fastest tier" instinct trades a verified composition for an unverified distributed system, and G2's one-provider-per-realm is the invariant that makes placement verifiable). Proposed shape, to be designed: a component-level placement annotation (e.g. `component HotWorker placed on rust` / a `placement` entry in the composition manifest) that the placement/emit pipeline lowers to per-component backend emission + the existing interop seam (item 56's bridge / 161-162's realm+router) for cross-tier calls — with G2/G3/G4 still checked over the WHOLE manifest, so a cross-tier component is admitted exactly like a cross-process one today. GATED on item 173 (go/java/wasm emitted-body routing needs the runtime liveness primitive first; py/ts/rust routing exists via item 167), and on the emit pipeline learning per-component backend selection (each `emit.py` today emits the whole document). Deliverable: one component placed on a second tier in a demo + a verification that the placed component's crossings ride the interop seam with G2/G3 intact. `src/revl/placement.py` + `backends/*/emit.py` (per-component backend routing) + `docs/distribution-model.md`. ~med; explicit placement, never auto.

364. ✅ LANDED 2026-08-31 (is_space/is_digit/is_alpha/is_alnum added to ts _ts_builtin, ASCII single-code-point semantics byte-identical to py/rust over all 256 bytes) **TS backend: the item-233 char-classification builtins (`is_space`/`is_digit`/`is_alpha`/`is_alnum`) typecheck but the ts emitter has no lowering — admitted program refused at emit, py/ts divergence (lighthouse-workload finding, paid twice).** Item 233 landed the builtins on py (`backends/python/emit.py`) and item 267 ported them to rust; the typescript emitter has NO case, so `s.charAt(i).is_space()` compiles clean, passes `revl test --backend py`, then `revl test --backend ts` dies with `emitter refused: unknown builtin method 'is_space'`. Repro is a two-line fn (verified on current main: `[py] pass` / `[ts] fail: emitter refused`). The workload paid this round-trip in two independent sessions (whitespace guards in an approval-gate helper and again in an authoring-reply trimmer), both rewritten to `charCodeAt` comparisons (space 32, tab 9, LF 10, CR 13). Fix: add the ts lowering mirroring py's native forms (a code-point range/set check, receiver-once), or refuse the builtins uniformly on the frontend for tiers without a lowering — the `EXPR_DISPATCHERS`/`EXPR_REFUSED` step-sync rule the agent guide already names. `backends/typescript/emit.py` + a ts run test per builtin. LOW effort, MED benefit (every scanner/trimmer in a dual-tier workload hits it).

365. ✅ LANDED 2026-08-31 (clear stray-backtick-closed-template diagnostic pointing at the real template + no-escape workaround; error-path only, additive) **DIAGNOSTIC: a stray backtick inside a backtick template (e.g. in an embedded host-JS comment) silently closes the template and the error surfaces far away, naming an unrelated identifier (lighthouse-workload finding, paid twice).** A revl backtick template holding a page's JavaScript is a load-bearing workload pattern; a contributor writing a JS comment like ``// read the `answer` field`` closes the template at the first embedded backtick, the template's tail reparses as revl declarations, and the diagnostic points at whatever identifier the tail happens to contain — verified on current main: a 6-line repro reports ``error: probe.rvl:3: `answer` is not declared in this function`` (G1) with no mention of the template. In the workload the same mistake surfaced as a RUNTIME `AttributeError` in a DIFFERENT component's lifecycle test, costing a four-file bisect; two sessions paid it independently. Fix: when a template literal's closing backtick leaves trailing content that fails to parse as declarations (or when a template closes mid-line inside a `//`/`/*` host-comment context), point the diagnostic at the template's opening/closing span — "template literal closed here; did you mean to embed a backtick?" — the way item 70 fixed the sibling brace-balancing trap. `src/revl/lexer.py`/`parser.py` (template capture + a boundary-aware secondary diagnostic). LOW effort, MED benefit (a 30-minute bisect becomes a one-line fix).


366. ✅ **Bitwise operators on Int32 (and Int) — a real language gap (found via the 272 crypto discussion).** revl has `Int32` (trapping arithmetic) but NO bitwise ops, so bit-manipulation kernels are inexpressible: SHA-256/HMAC (rotate/shift/xor/and), masks, bitsets, flags, packing. This is why stdlib/crypto had to be host `@py`/`@ts` externs instead of pure revl. Add `&` (AND), `|` (OR), `^` (XOR), `~` (NOT unary), `<<` (shl), `>>` (shr) on Int32 - and decide Int (64-bit two's complement) support. Semantics: bitwise ops do NOT trap (bit patterns, not arithmetic); define shift-by->=width (0 or trap - decide); `>>` on Int32 is arithmetic or logical (decide, document). Cross-tier: every tier has native bitwise (py `&|^~<<>>`, ts number/bigint, rust, java, go, wasm `i32.and/or/xor/shl/shr_s|u`) so lowering is clean; conformance/byte-identity per tier. UNBLOCKS a pure-revl SHA-256/HMAC (all six tiers uniform) and any numeric kernel. `src/revl/{parser,typecheck,lower}.py` + all six backends/*/emit.py + docs/arithmetic.md.


367. ✅ **A TOTAL (never-raising) FIELD READ on a parsed value — 362 made the PARSE total, but reading a field off the parsed record still raises on py and silently yields `undefined` on ts, so no tolerant JSON WALK is expressible dual-tier (revl-harness lane H24, the direct follow-on to 362; probe-verified on `07bf23f`, re-verified unchanged after item 361 landed).** Item 362 landed `json_try_parse(s) -> Result[Any, Str]` and its closing claim was that the harness could then do "per-engine field reads off the parsed record, which typed access already supports". That claim holds only when every key is PRESENT. A real provider reply is exactly the case where it is not: `usage` may be absent, `choices[0].message.tool_calls` may be absent, `reasoning` may be spelled `reasoning_content`, and the whole document may not even be an object. Reading an ABSENT key off a value bound from `Any` diverges by tier — py raises, ts returns `undefined`:

    ```revl
    use "stdlib/json.rvl" { json_try_parse }
    type EOpt = { kind: Opt[Str] }
    pub fn a(s: Str) -> Str {
      return match json_try_parse(s) { Ok(v) => f(v), Err(e) => "ERR" }
    }
    fn f(v: Any) -> Str {
      let e: EOpt = v
      return e.kind ?? "<none>"          // the designed spelling for "may be absent"
    }
    test "optional field read off a parsed record" {
      assert a("""{"kind":"final"}""") == "final"
      assert a("""{"other":1}""")      == "<none>"    // py: KeyError 'kind'  ts: passes
    }
    ```

    Verified on current main: `[ts] pass` / `[py] fail: KeyError: 'kind'`. The cause is one line — `backends/python/emit.py` emits `_revl_field(v, name)` = `v[name] if isinstance(v, dict) else getattr(v, name)`, a TOTAL read on neither branch, while `backends/typescript/emit.py::_member` emits plain `target.name`, which is total by JS accident. So the two tiers disagree in BOTH directions: for an `Opt[T]`-declared field ts is right and py raises; for a plainly-typed `Str` field ts is SILENTLY wrong (`undefined` flows on as a value — the same silent class item 279 fixed for reserved-word keys, and the same class item 299 then audited across the other tiers) while py at least fails loudly.

    There is no dual-tier workaround. `Map[Str, Str]` binding + `has`/`lookup` is total on py but dies on ts with `m.has is not a function` (a JSON object is a plain `Object`, not a JS `Map`; the binding is a type-erased cast, not a conversion), and `Any` has no `has` at all (`builtin `has` needs a Map receiver, got `Any``). So a component still cannot express "read this field if it is there" — which is what EVERY tolerant JSON walk is made of.

    Proposed fix, in preference order: (1) make an `Opt[T]`-declared field read TOTAL on every tier — py emits `.get(name)` / `getattr(v, name, None)`, ts keeps `?.`, the statically-typed tiers get the equivalent — so `e.kind ?? default` is the one designed spelling for "may be absent" and it means the same thing everywhere; (2) decide and unify the NON-`Opt` case, which is the 279/299 silent-divergence class: either both tiers raise, or the frontend refuses a non-`Opt` field read on a value whose static type is `Any`, so the author is pushed to (1); (3) optionally give `Any` a total `has`/`lookup` pair so a shape can be discriminated before it is bound. Related, same root: there is no way to ask whether a parsed `Any` is an object, a list, or a scalar — the harness's externs all begin with `isinstance(d, dict)`, which is currently inexpressible.

    **What it is holding hostage, concretely (all measured in revl-harness lane H24, all blocked by THIS, not by 362):** 5 hand-rolled tolerant-parse externs whose @py+@ts bodies exist only to do `d.get(k)` with a default — `parse_envelope` (agent.rvl, the reply-decode floor), `parse_usage` / `answer_key` / `extract_reply` / `extract_reasoning` (real_model.rvl, provider usage + reasoning-model prose), `parse_tool_key` (cost_ledger.rvl) — plus `wire_text_or_empty` (self_evolver/guarded_dynamic_toolbox) and the protocol-decode half of `tools/mcp_client.py` (268 lines: `reply.get("id")`, `"error" in reply`, `result.get("content")`, `c.get("type") == "text"` — every line an optional field read). 362 removed the parse half of the wall; this item is the other half, and until it lands the decode POLICY cannot leave host code no matter how total the parse is. `backends/python/emit.py` (`_revl_field`) + `backends/typescript/emit.py` (`_member`) + `src/revl/typecheck.py` (the `Any`-receiver field rule) + the other four tiers + a cross-tier conformance test per shape (present / absent / wrong-typed / non-object). ~small-med; it is the completion of 362, not a new surface.

369. ✅ **WITNESSED INVERSES REPLAY IN REGISTRATION ORDER, NOT LIFO — abort can leave residue or DESTROY pre-session data, and item 244's `stdlib/fs.rvl` reproduces it in three lines (found in revl-harness lane H10; DATA LOSS, contradicts G7 and docs/design/243-witnessed-externs.md §2).** A witnessed effect is auto-approvable *only* because abort provably reverts it — that is the whole argument of 243/246, and it is what item 244's catalog and the harness's H1/H10 lanes sell to an operator. On the py reference tier the promise currently holds only while a session's witnessed ops touch DISJOINT paths: inverses registered from **provide-METHOD invocations** (i.e. every witnessed effect an agent tool fires mid-session, as opposed to one fired from an activation body) replay in REGISTRATION order rather than LIFO, so two ops whose paths overlap undo in the wrong order. Measured on `608358c`, py tier, each case a single component and — in the last two — a *single method*, so this is not cross-component teardown ordering, it is the frame's replay order:

    ```
    # via a consumer of stdlib/fs.rvl + stdlib/shell.rvl (revl-harness H10)
    mv a.txt b.txt ; mv b.txt c.txt ; abort  -> leaves b.txt   (should be a.txt)
    rm a.txt       ; touch a.txt   ; abort   -> a.txt is GONE  (pre-session data)

    # via stdlib/fs.rvl alone (revl-harness H1, already landed and shipping):
    write a.txt "V2" ; write a.txt "V3" ; abort
        -> a.txt == "V2"   (should be the pre-session "V1")
    ```

    Read the third one twice: two ordinary writes to one file, then an abort, and the workspace is left holding an intermediate version **that never existed before the session** — neither the pre-session bytes nor the last write. LIFO gives the pre-session bytes; FIFO replays `restore(preimage=V1)` first (correct) and then `restore(preimage=V2)` over the top (wrong). `mv a b ; mv b c` is the cleanest reproducer of all: one method, one op, two invocations — LIFO would `unmove(c->b)` then `unmove(b->a)` and land on `a.txt`; the observed `b.txt` is exactly the FIFO order. Every `stdlib/fs.rvl` inverse is written idempotent-and-total (`if os.path.exists(...)`, docs' "a second replay is a no-op"), which is right, and it is also what turns the wrong ORDER into a SILENT wrong result instead of an error: the inverse that runs too early finds nothing and no-ops, and the one that runs after it undoes into the hole.

    What it contradicts: **G7 (LIFO teardown)** and `docs/design/243-witnessed-externs.md` §2, "Slice 2a as implemented" — *"`Frame.transactional(undo, witness)` returns a `_Transactional` disposer that joins the same LIFO disposer stack as every bracket inverse (so mixed-entry LIFO is preserved for free)"*. That paragraph reasons about the ACTIVATION body, whose disposers cordis unwinds LIFO on the setup-failure path; effects fired LATER, from provide-method calls on an ACTIVE component, appear to append to a list that is drained forward. Whether the bug is in the accumulator, in the abort drain, or in the contract's silence about the mid-session case is the first thing to determine — the design doc never states which order a post-activation witnessed effect unwinds in, and the answer has to be LIFO for the guarantee to mean anything.

    Why it matters beyond a tidiness bug: 246 auto-approves class (a) crossings **silently, with no prompt**, on the strength of the checked inverse. An out-of-order replay means the runtime silently auto-approved something it cannot revert — the exact failure the classification exists to prevent, and the one an agent harness cannot detect from the outside (abort reports `noResidue: true`; the tree is simply wrong). It is worse than an emission that prompts.

    Cost already paid downstream, as evidence of severity: revl-harness lane H10 could not ship 252's payoff without a **replay-order guard** in its own component — every witnessed arm claims the paths its inverse will touch (both endpoints for `mv`, the target for `rm`/`mkdir`/`cp`/`touch`, ancestor/descendant-aware), and a SECOND witnessed op on a claimed path is routed to the honest `emission` instead. That is the safe direction (a false emission costs a prompt; a false witness auto-approves the irreversible), but the cost is that the most ordinary chained flows an agent writes — `touch a` then `mv a b`, `mkdir d` then `cp x d/y` — now prompt, which is most of what 252 was meant to stop prompting. The guard is written to be deleted the day this lands, and the lane's exit test uses an interleaved `mv a b ; mv b c` so it notices. Lane H1's already-landed `witnessed_fs_toolbox.rvl` has NO such guard and its FEATURES row promises the pre-session tree unqualified — so this is shipping today.

    Exit: a witnessed effect fired from a provide method registers a disposer that replays in reverse INVOCATION order across the whole frame, proven by the three reproducers above plus a mixed bracket/transactional case (243 §2's "mixed-entry LIFO" claim, tested rather than asserted); the mid-session ordering is written into `docs/design/243-witnessed-externs.md` so the contract stops being silent about the case every agent tool is in; conformance across the tiers that carry Slice 2b. `backends/python/runtime.py` (`Frame.transactional` / the abort drain) + `backends/python/emit.py` if registration is the culprit, the other tiers' teardown loops, `docs/design/243-witnessed-externs.md`, and a `stdlib/fs.rvl` test per reproducer. **HIGH — it is a correctness hole under the guarantee 243/244/246 are built to sell, and it is reachable from the stdlib catalog in three lines.** See revl-harness FEEDBACK F-H10.7.

373. ✅ LANDED 2026-08-30 (extern emission(confined: param) reach declaration; revl audit names the reach) **The audit surface names a crossing but cannot name its REACH — a confined emission and an unconfined one are indistinguishable on G8 (found in revl-harness lane R-3).** The harness spawns a coding-agent CLI as its chat provider through one `extern emission fn engine_run(argv_json, env_json, cwd, timeout_s, sandbox_mode)`. R-3 changed that spawn from "inherits the harness's ambient authority, cwd defaults to the process cwd (the repo — it wrote `src/plugins/bitcoin_price.rvl` into a live checkout)" to "cwd is a canonicalized workspace that is refused if it sits inside a harness checkout, and the process runs under a deny-all-`file-write*` macOS seatbelt profile with a narrow allowlist plus an explicit trailing deny of the checkout". `revl audit` prints, before and after, the identical line: `engine_run [emission] backends: py, ts`. The classification is right (the process runs; nothing un-runs it) and 252 already gets the crossing NAMED — but the review surface that is supposed to be the differentiator cannot see the one property a reviewer most needs: what the crossing was BOUNDED to. A reader infers confinement only by noticing the suggestively-named neighbours (`engine_workspace_root [emission]`, `engine_workspace_scan [pure]`, `engine_residue_report [pure]`), never by reading a declaration. Ask: let an emission declare its reach — e.g. `extern emission(confined: workspace) fn …`, or a `reach` clause the checker records and `audit` prints — with `audit --diff` flagging a WEAKENING (confined → unconfined) the way it flags a new crossing today. Semantics to decide: is the declaration a claim the host body is trusted to honour (like the classification itself, honest-by-review) or something the checker can partially verify (e.g. the confinement argument must be a parameter, not a literal fallback)? Even the trust-me version is worth having: a weakened reach becomes a reviewable diff instead of a comment in a host body, and the honest limitation moves out of prose (`docs/threat-model.md`) onto the surface. Same family as 252 — 252 asks that the crossing be named, this asks that its reach be named. Secondary friction from the same lane, worth a line here: revl has no host-body fragment/include, so the ~60-line seatbelt mechanism is copy-pasted FOUR times (`engine_run` @py/@ts, `engine_run_sync` @py/@ts); for a security mechanism that copy-paste is a liability, because a jail that silently drifts between the async and sync spawn is exactly the bug a diff review misses. `src/revl/{parser,typecheck}.py` + `tools/audit`.

379. ✅ IMPLEMENTED 2026-08-30 (break/continue landed on all six tiers, frame-neutral by construction with a whole-IR enforcement pass, Fable review corrections C1-C4; self-host port pending as item 391; supersedes the flag-guarded-header framing below) **No `break`/`continue` in loops — early exit must be a flag-guarded loop header (found in the 276 lexer perf work; ergonomics + agent-first-try correctness + a modest hot-loop speedup).** revl has `while`/`for` but NO `break`/`continue` (confirmed: none in parser/lexer), so a loop that decides mid-body to stop must set a `done`/`handled`/`isf` flag the header re-checks (seen throughout selfhost/lexer.rvl's 18 loops). Three costs: (a) ERGONOMICS/CORRECTNESS - flag boilerplate is a bug class (forget to set it / wrong re-check); (b) AGENT-FIRST-TRY - `break` is muscle-memory in every language, so an agent AUTHORING revl reaches for it first, hits a parse error, and must rework into a flag loop; a real first-try correctness tax on the harness-dogfood story; (c) PERF (modest, NOT a silver bullet) - a flag-guarded early-exit loop pays a per-iteration boolean check plus one redundant final iteration; `break` removes both. Scan-while-condition loops (most of the lexer's 18) already put the exit in the header and gain nothing, so sell it as ergonomics+correctness and BENCH-GATE the perf claim (contrast 276, which removes an ALLOCATION per byte - a bigger lever; break removes a compare, not an allocation). DESIGN CATCH (the correctness-careful part): revl's differentiator is VERIFIED LIFO TEARDOWN - a `break`/`continue` (or early `return`) out of a scope that acquired resources must still unwind that scope's disposers correctly. Pure code (the lexer) is trivial; effectful code needs teardown-across-early-exit to be SOUND or the guarantee breaks. Scope: `break`/`continue` in `while`/`for` - frontend `src/revl/{parser,typecheck,lower,emission_analysis}.py` + effect analysis for teardown-on-exit + all six `backends/*/emit.py`, bench-gated on the selfhost lexer; pairs with 276. DESIGN-FIRST on the teardown-across-early-exit semantics.

380. ✅ **String interpolation in a non-backtick string is SILENT-WRONG, and it exposes a type-checker SOUNDNESS HOLE (LLM-authorability audit; HIGH — silent miscompile + unsound return typing).** A model writes `"hi ${name}"` or `f"hi {name}"` by muscle memory. Observed on main: `"hi ${name}"` compiles clean (exit 0) and emits the LITERAL `${name}` — silent wrong output. `f"hi {name}"` parses as `return f` (the identifier) plus a dead string statement; when an `f` is in scope it SILENTLY MISCOMPILES to exit 0, returning the function value where a `Str` was declared and passing the checker unchecked — a real return-type soundness hole (`return <function-name>` type-checks as any declared return type). Two fixes: (a) a diagnostic that flags `${` or `{ident}` inside a `"`-string and a leading `f"` (redirect to a backtick template `` `hi ${name}` ``, per §0/§10 exclusion-diagnostic philosophy); (b) CLOSE the checker hole so `return <function-value>` where a non-function type is declared is refused. `src/revl/{lexer,parser,typecheck}.py`. Silent-wrong + unsound = top priority.

Observed: the number lexer (`src/revl/lexer.py`) lex-splits `0xFF` into int `0` + ident `xFF`, producing the MISLEADING `` `xFF` is not declared … declare it with `let` `` (G1) — a nonsensical redirect. Add `0x`/`0b`/`0o` prefixes and `_` digit separators to the number lexer. Pure lexer change, no semantic conflict, high frequency in generated numeric/bit code (pairs with item 366 bitwise). `src/revl/lexer.py`.

382. ✅ LANDED 2026-08-30 (single-quoted string/char literals in the lexer, byte-identical) **Single-quoted string / char literals — `'a'` / `'hello'` (LLM-authorability audit; cheap lexer sugar).** Both Python and JS accept single-quoted strings; extremely high frequency. Observed: `error: unexpected character "'"` — cryptic, no redirect. revl has no char type, so a single-quoted literal maps naturally to a 1-char (or n-char) `Str`. Fix: lex `'...'` as a `Str` (consistent with revl already dual-spelling `==`/`===` for exactly this muscle-memory reason), or at minimum redirect the lex error to `"`. `src/revl/lexer.py`.

390. ✅ LANDED 2026-08-30 (exported json-tagged struct fields, cross-tier bytes match py/ts, real-Go exec verified) **go emitter: a revl record lowers to a Go struct with UNEXPORTED fields and no `json:` tags, so `encoding/json` drops them — `json_stringify(record)` returns `{}` on the go tier (found in item 385).** Item 385 made `json_stringify` byte-identical across tiers for scalars/strings/lists, but on go a RECORD stringifies to `{}` because the Go struct fields are lowercase/unexported and carry no `json:"name"` tag, so `encoding/json` silently omits them. 391. **🚧 PARTIAL (2 slices landed, the gap is now MEASURED not estimated) — SELF-HOST PARITY CATCH-UP; PO DECISION: the self-host is a FULL CURRENT-LANGUAGE compiler for v3, not a subset proof.** The differential byte-agreement oracles (tests/test_selfhost_{lexer,parser,checker,lower,emit_*}.py) prevent SILENT divergence on the corpus but do NOT force new features in — a feature the corpus does not exercise leaves the oracle green while the self-host lacks it. **THE MEASUREMENT (2026-09-02, on `00bf8336`), which replaces this item's earlier estimate.** Two numbers, both produced by running the reference and the self-host over the SAME inputs rather than by reading code: (a) *gate parity* — over all 122 `examples/rejections/*.rvl` fixtures, `selfhost/lower.rvl`'s `admit_src` agreed with the reference on tag AND message for **17**; it FALSE-ADMITTED **87** (it raised no objection at all to a program the reference refuses) and gave a different message on 18. (b) *lexer parity* — over all 862 reference-lexable `.rvl` files in the tree (not the 8-file oracle corpus), `selfhost/lexer.rvl` diverged on **9**, and 6 of those 9 were SELF-HOST SOURCES: the self-host lexer could not lex `selfhost/{lower,emit_go,emit_java,emit_py,emit_rust,emit_wasm}.rvl`. This item's original claim ("does not lex 0x/<</&") was already stale — hex/bin/oct, `_` grouping, single quotes, `& | ^ ~ << >>` and the `break`/`continue` keywords all lex correctly. The real lexer defect was elsewhere and invisible to the corpus: the `"` spelling ran an escape-BLIND scanner (item 382 gave the `'` spelling the escapes and left `"` behind), and the raw-brace balancers counted braces inside strings — which is exactly why a self-host source full of `\"`-built JSON could not be lexed by the self-host. **THE TYPE LAYER IS A DISTINCT, LARGE SUB-GOAL, NOT ONE MORE PORT SLICE (item 417).** Of the 87 false-admits measured above, ~40 are T1/T2 type errors and there is NO type layer in the self-host at all: `admit_src` decides the composition/guarantee layer (G1..G4, A1, PRELUDE, ROUTE, SPAWN, HANDOFF, BAD) and nothing else. That sub-goal gets its own slices (type environment, expression typing, return-path totality, generic instantiation, Int32 width rules, match exhaustiveness, the stdlib method surface), its own corpus family, and it must NOT be folded into the per-feature port list below. **LANDED SO FAR** (`fix/391-selfhost-parity`): the foreign-construct redirect table (384) — all 21 `examples/rejections/foreign_*.rvl` fixtures now refuse with the reference's message byte-for-byte, under the new `FOREIGN` tag, taking the false-admit count 87 → 67; and the lexer's string-escape + string-aware brace balancing, taking lexer parity 853/862 → 861/862 (the self-host can now lex every self-host source). **STILL OPEN**, measured: 67 false-admits and 17 message divergences over the rejection corpus, of which the largest families are the type layer (~40, see 417), the `lifecycle test` block surface (6, unparsed), extern `undo`/`compensate` slot validation (5), module-fn scope resolution and `let`-reassignment (5), the stdlib method surface (3), `use`-module resolution (3), match exhaustiveness, `verified` totality, and the Int-literal 64-bit range check (which currently CRASHES the gate with an OverflowError rather than refusing). THE PAYOFF (why this is more than parity-for-its-own-sake): once ported, the self-host's OWN SOURCE gets to USE the new features — bitwise in the lexer hot path, .map/.filter/break to simplify the compiler code, single-quote/hex literals, canonical json, the total field read — so it is real dogfooding that makes the self-host source cleaner and faster, and every new feature is exercised by the compiler that most stresses it. PORT each remaining feature into selfhost/{lexer,parser,checker,lower,emit_*}.rvl and EXTEND the corpus: .map/.filter/.reduce + comprehension redirect (383); Value dot-accessors (189); total field read + Any-shape (367/H24); json_try_parse (362) + canonical json_stringify (385); string-interp + return-type-hole diagnostics (380); extern config{} coeffect (378); emission[caps] (343) + emission(confined) reach (373); async effect composition (131); sync/async arrow poly (342); async match-block arm (361); admit crossing (330); multi-error reporting (386); the per-backend host-body trivia tables (`_HOST_TRIVIA`: `'` char/rune and string literals, `/* */` and wasm `(; ;)` block comments, Python triple quotes — only the `"` span is ported). Slice by stage where a feature is stage-local, vertically (all stages) where it is not. Multi-wave. STANDING PROCESS: every future reference-side language feature includes a 'does this need a self-host port?' step and files the port slice if yes. NOTE for the next slice: a new verdict tag (this pass added `FOREIGN`) is invisible to the oracle until `tests/test_selfhost_lower.py`'s `_classify` learns the family — that classifier work belongs to item 429, so a port that introduces a tag pins itself with in-file `test` blocks and says so. selfhost/*.rvl + tests/test_selfhost_*.py (extend corpus). Relates to 417 (the type layer), 429 (corpus coverage), 146 (full self-host).

411. ◑ SLICE 1 LANDED 2026-08-31 (STATIC sandbox placement: [processes.X.sandbox] + [tiers]-form [sandbox] surface, expand_tiers split into sandbox_<component>, both-forms refusal, sandbox-table validation, the [sandbox.needs] fail-closed gate for a need outside the fs/net vocabulary, per-process config/spec narrowing so secrets do not enter the boundary, boot-summary + `revl audit --placement` envelope view, swap refusal; merged 09d1821, 28 tests. SLICE 2 remaining = the RUNTIME driver: container/microVM/wasm-cell launch + health + teardown, the in-sandbox boot canary, the per-rung transport variant, and the conductor-served approval-across-boundary channel; needs Docker/wasm at runtime.) DESIGN DONE + adversarial review folded 2026-08-31 (docs/design/411-sandbox-placement.md: sandbox as a 4th placement column over the 363 seam, plan-time cap gate + trusted-runtime enforcer, wasm-cell/container/microvm ladder, mixed-arch, makes 329/249 enforced; open Q = cap-name<->OS-resource vocabulary bridge) **Capability-enforced sandbox placement — a component runs in its own isolation boundary (wasm cell / container / microVM) with a declared capability envelope enforced at RUNTIME, still composed with unsandboxed components over the 363 seam.** Extends item-363 per-component placement from "which tier" to "which isolation + capability envelope": a component declares no-disk/no-net (or an allowlist) and runs in `docker run --network=none --read-only` / a microVM / a wasm cell, communicating with the rest of the composition over the EXISTING 363 proxy/stub seam (value-copy, G8 allowlist, seam deadlines, peer-death-as-withdrawal = container-death) across the isolation boundary. The sandbox is the RUNTIME ENFORCEMENT of the statically-declared capability envelope (`emission[caps]` / attenuation / item 289 host-imports-subset-of-caps): a component whose declared caps EXCEED the sandbox grant is refused at plan time (like 363's tier-capability gate). SECURITY PAYOFF: makes item 329 (untrusted author) + item 249 (taint) ENFORCED not just checked — an opaque/malicious host body confined to `--network=none` physically cannot exfiltrate whatever G8 cannot see inside it. USE CASE: mixed-arch compositions — a foreign-arch binary wrapped as a revl component runs in a container of that arch (multi-arch image / qemu) and talks to the host composition over the arch-agnostic (serialized-value) seam. TRUST BOUNDARY: revl DECLARES + REQUESTS the confinement and refuses caps that exceed the grant, but the container runtime is a trusted enforcer (revl cannot verify Docker actually applied --network=none), the way the OS is today. Cross-sandbox witnessed rollback + cross-tier determinism scoped out (like 363). The conductor gains a sandbox-runtime driver (launch/health/teardown). 420. ✅ **LANDED 2026-09-02** (all four exit conditions: (a)-(c) at `233352e9`, composed with item 423 on `fix/420-423-composed`; (d) on `fix/420d-undo-rejected-diagnostic`). (a) site-undo arguments are arity- and type-checked through the same core as the extern slot, in all four site slots (activation-body `effect`, provide-method `effect`/`let`-effect, `subscribe`, `emit ... compensate`); (b) the legal seam spelling is `witnessed`, and the refusal now names it; (c) O1's hint is corrected for the position it fires in. The composition kept ONE judgment with TWO hints: 423's construction-time check is the only argument judgment on the component stratum and carries the slot on `env`, so the message line is the stratum checker's verbatim in every position (T1 classification never depends on position) and only the hint varies. 423's construction-time check SUBSUMES this item's post-lowering sweep, which was removed: construction also reaches calls nested under an opaque host `call` node whose arguments `infer_ir` will not visit, and reports at the inner call's own line rather than the step's. (d) the "has no undo" diagnostic no longer denies a declared `undo`. Reproduced first: `extern acquire fn open_h() -> H undo close_h(result)` plus `let h = effect open_h()` reported `effect has no \`undo\` and \`open_h\` is not pure` with the declaration two lines up. The refusal STANDS (a non-`witnessed` extern's declared inverse is never replayed by either tier, so the teardown that actually runs on abort is the site undo and there was none), but the reason it gives is now the true one: ``effect has no site `undo`: `open_h` declares `undo close_h(...)`, but an `acquire` extern's declared inverse is never replayed``, hinting the two fixes that were VERIFIED to compile (spell the inverse at the site, or classify the extern `witnessed` so the declared one replays, which requires a `Result[Witness, Error]` return). The generic wording's third escape, `emit`, is deliberately dropped from the specific hint: `emit` marks an `emission` crossing and an `acquire` extern cannot be emitted (both `let h = emit open_h()` and bare `emit open_h()` are themselves refused, checked), so offering it would be advice the author cannot take (item 274). Composed the way (a)-(c) were, as ONE judgment: the message table is a single renderer (`parser.missing_undo_refusal`) that both raising positions call, specific where the caller can supply the rejected declaration and generic otherwise. **Both spellings were live, and both are fixed.** `lower.py`'s copy runs on the merged, post-import program and is the only one that can know an extern's classification (item 315's deferral is exactly that), so it renders the specific message. `parser.py`'s copy fires where it can prove the acquisition is not a bare name, but a bare NAME (`effect open_h`, no parens) reached it and named a declared extern, so the parser's deferral was widened from `ExprCall(ExprVar)` to `ExprVar` too: its domain is now only shapes that cannot be an extern (dotted path, literal, operator), where "has no `undo`" is the truth. **Self-host check (item 429 exit (1)), done against the source, not the oracle:** `selfhost/checker.rvl` does not model this refusal at all. Its extern record is `mk_fn_d(name, params, isEmission)` (`p_extern`), which keeps no classification beyond emission-or-not and no declared `undo`, and no `has no \`undo\`` text exists anywhere in `selfhost/`. So there is nothing to keep verbatim, and no port: mirroring the new message would mean first porting the whole extern-classification-and-declared-inverse model, which is a feature port, not the diagnostic-text mirroring 429 asks for. The `{ ctx, env, ev, msg }` diagnostic type would in any case carry only the message line, not the hint that does the navigational work here. **THE SITE `undo` SLOT IS NOT ARGUMENT-CHECKED, and item 308 has no legal spelling at a provide-method seam.** (Found by the revl-harness item-308 migration, 2026-09-02; reproduced and widened here.) Three shapes COMPILE on main today against `extern pure fn secret_release(h: SecretHandle)`: `undo secret_release("a plain Str")` (wrong type), `undo secret_release(42)` (wrong type), and `undo secret_release(1, 2, 3)` (**wrong ARITY**, which the consumer had not even found). Meanwhile `_check_extern_undo` (`lower.py:1865`) checks the extern's own declared slot properly: callee-is-declared, no self-reference, arity and argument types against the declared signature with `result: T` in scope.
    **Why this is severe rather than cosmetic:** an acquire extern's DECLARED `undo` is never replayed on either tier (`ext["undo"]` is read in exactly four places, all item-243 witnessed emitters). The teardown that actually RUNS is the site undo. So the code that executes on every abort, while the activation is already unwinding, is unchecked for arity and types, and fails at runtime at the worst possible moment.
    **The design half.** At a provide-method seam item 308's identity guarantee has no legal spelling: the acquire's result cannot be bound (only `spawn` may be acquired there), `result` is not in scope in a site undo (unlike the extern slot, where it is the one implicit binding), and re-minting a same-typed handle is correctly refused by O1. So the ONLY shape that compiles at a seam is the one that LAUNDERS the type, which is exactly what 308 exists to prevent. Closing the checking hole without providing a legal spelling would make a legitimate pattern unwritable. The consumer's own resolution is the candidate answer: the seam releases through a DECLARED crossing that re-derives the handle and delegates, so there is one delete mechanism and it is on the audit surface.
    **O1's hint is unactionable in that position** (item 274's standard is that a refusal names a fix the author can enact).
    **A related diagnostic defect, found while probing:** with a nominal acquire return whose site undo does not close the bound handle, the compiler reports `effect has no 'undo' and <fn> is not pure` even though an `undo` IS declared. The message denies the existence of something the author wrote, which sends them looking in the wrong place. It should say the undo was rejected and why.
    Exit: site-undo arguments arity- and type-checked through the SAME core as the extern slot, covering bound/unbound effects, activation and provide-method bodies, and the `subscribe ... undo ...` slot; a legal, documented spelling for releasing an acquired handle at a provide-method seam; O1's hint corrected for the position it fires in; and the "has no undo" diagnostic corrected. All four met; see the mark above for where each landed.

421. **CAPABILITY / CODEGEN / SEAM AUDIT (2026-09-02, item 416f surfaces).** Eight proven findings, all with executed reproducers. Fix status noted per item.
    **F1 CRITICAL, ✅ FIXED 2026-09-02** (`4e818869`, `fix/f1-capability-token-attenuation`). `_cap_keyed` (`src/revl/lower.py:10210`) now keys the fold element by the DECLARED capability token, read from the same source of truth `parallel._resolve_emission` uses for the same crossings, so `_check_spawn_attenuation` compares capability BOUNDARIES instead of wiring-key spellings. A boundary that no declaration tokens (an `emission` method with no capability list, an unresolvable service) is still named by its G2 wiring key but in its own token namespace, so a key spelling can never be mistaken for a declared token, and a malformed stored spelling degrades to `*`, fail-closed on both sides. The fixture-rename reproducer is pinned in `tests/test_spawn_attenuation.py`. Original finding: `lower.py:9487` `_cap_keyed` DISCARDS the declared capability token and keys the `Cap` by the component's own local `requires` key spelling, so `_check_spawn_attenuation` (`:9791`) compares identifier spellings that name nothing in common. The project's own fixture `examples/rejections/g4_spawn_widens_capability.rvl` is defeated by renaming the child's `requires` key from `kv_b` to `kv_a`: BASELINE refuses, ATTACK is ADMITTED with `"holds": ["kv_a"], "granted": ["kv_a"], "attenuated": []`. Strongest form: a parent holding a PURE non-emission service under key `notes`, child wires `notes` to `emission[fs.write(path="/etc")]`, and the emitted python performs the `/etc` crossing while the G8 audit surface attests `attenuated: ["notes"]`. Violates the guarantee `lower.py:9793` states in its own comment (items 66/294). The data is available and the loss is deliberate: `parallel.py:104` `_resolve_emission` reads the real declared tokens for the same crossings, which is why `disjoint`/`parallel.py` is sound. Only interactive deployments have a second control (`mcp/session.py:37` `_cap_covers`); a compiled artifact has none. `test_spawn_attenuation.py` / `test_parameterized_capabilities.py` / `test_budget_260.py` were 36/36 green while this worked.
    **F2 HIGH, ✅ FIXED 2026-09-02** (`4e818869`, same branch). The ceiling rule is now CONE-SCOPED and EXISTENTIAL (`_ceiling_attenuation_check`, `src/revl/lower.py:10524-10555`): the only held caps that can license a child crossing are those whose resource-only projection covers the crossing's own cone (`cap_order.split_ceilings` plus the stripped-pair `covers` test), and ONE single held cap must license the whole crossing, binding every ceiling at-or-above the child's. The per-token `max()` is gone, and so is the per-parameter `max` over covering caps, which would have been the same unsoundness one level in. Original finding: `lower.py:9789-9795` `_ceiling_attenuation_check` aggregates the parent budget per bare token with `max()`, discarding the resource cone: a parent holding `fs(calls=1,path="/a")` and `fs(calls=100,path="/b")` admits a child granted `fs(calls=100,path="/a")`, a 100x budget on the cone where the parent holds 1. The docstring calls `max` "the conservative first cut"; it is conservative in the unsound direction.
    **F3 HIGH, ✅ FIXED 2026-09-02** (`67fc1b53`, `fix/injective-identifier-mangling`). The reserved-word rename is injective on ALL FIVE tiers now, by the same rule everywhere: escape a name iff the name OR any name reachable from it by dropping trailing `_` is reserved, and escape it by exactly one `_`, which shifts the whole `kw`/`kw_`/`kw__` ladder up one rung and leaves every other name verbatim. Verified present in `backends/python/emit.py:278-289`, `backends/typescript/emit.py:232-243`, `backends/go/emit.py:295-306`, `backends/java/emit.py:289-299` and `backends/rust/emit.py:705-715`. The self-host emitters were ported with it (item 429(b)), but item 429(c) is a DIFFERENT defect, the reserved-word SET rather than the mangling rule, and is NOT closed by this: see its own marker. Original finding: The keyword-mangling rename is NOT injective (`backends/python/emit.py:279`, and the same shape in ts/go/java): `lambda` maps to `lambda_` and a distinct identifier `lambda_` maps to `lambda_`. On PYTHON this silently captures: a function whose revl semantics return `PUBLIC-VALUE` returns `SEKRIT-CANARY` in emitted code. Top-level fns collide the same way, changing the module's exported API; record fields collide while the literal keeps the RAW key.
